headline: A traveler gave his passcode and his phone erased itself

sources.title: US accuses American of allegedly wiping his phone using a 'duress' password during border search
Border agents can lie to search your phone, but wiping your own data could land you in prison
Traveler Gave CBP A Passcode That Wiped His Phone At Atlanta Airport. Now He Faces Five Years In Prison

chunks.text: Samuel Tunick landed in Atlanta in January 2025 on a [[flight]] from the Dominican Republic. [[Customs]] officers {{pulled him aside}} for a second check and asked him to {{hand over}} the [[passcode]] to his phone. He gave them a code. The screen [[went dark]], [[flashed]] a few times, and the phone appeared to restart. The code he had typed was a [[duress]] code, and it {{wiped out}} everything on the device.

chunks.text: A duress code is a second passcode that the owner {{sets up}} in advance. When it is typed, it looks exactly like the real one, but instead of opening the phone it orders a [[factory reset]] and destroys the [[encryption]] keys, so the phone {{starts up}} clean and the old files cannot be read. The feature exists to {{keep out}} anyone who forces the owner to unlock a phone, and it is built into GrapheneOS, an [[operating system]] that some people install on their phones in place of the one that comes with them.

chunks.text: The stop happened in January 2025, but the case only became public in July 2026, and it is being fought in court now. [[Prosecutors]] have charged Tunick with destroying property to stop it being [[seized]], a rarely used law that carries up to five years in prison. He has pleaded not [[guilty]]. The officers said they were looking for illegal images, but they gave no reason for that [[suspicion]], and Tunick's [[lawyers]] say they had [[nothing to go on]]. They want a [[judge]] to {{throw out}} the [[evidence]] the officers gathered that day, and they argue that the stop would never {{stand up in court}} if the same thing had happened on a street rather than at an airport.

verbs.wrong: To return property to its owner

verbs.correct: To be accepted as valid by a judge
verbs.wrong: To be argued by a lawyer in person

chunks.text: The case {{comes down to}} an old question with a new object at the center of it. Courts have long allowed officers at a border to search a bag without a [[warrant]], and the government says a phone is no different. Lawyers who work on [[privacy]] say a phone holds a person's whole life, so {{going through}} one is not like opening a suitcase. [[Congress]] has never {{stepped in}} to write a clear rule, and no court has {{sorted out}} the question for good. Until one does, every traveler who is asked for a passcode is standing in the same [[gray area]] Tunick stood in.
